card.title: Potential Difference, Potential Due to a Point Charge, Potential Energy and Electron Volt

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Electrostatic potential V is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge from infinity, given by V = -∫E·dr, with SI unit the volt. A point charge Q produces V = kQ/r, falling as 1/r (compared with the field's 1/r²), and fields and potentials are linked by E = -∇V.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Potential: $V = \frac{W}{q_0} = -\int_\infty^P \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$
Potential difference: $\Delta V = V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$
Potential due to point charge: $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r} = k\frac{Q}{r}$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Treating potential as a vector and adding components: Potential V is a scalar. Only in a region with a clear directional symmetry (e.g. along the axis of a line charge) is it meaningful to write $V = -Ex$; you must never resolve V into vector components like x, y, z components.  ·  Confusing potential difference with potential: Potential difference is a change $\Delta V = V_B - V_A$ between two points and can be positive or negative. Potential V itself is defined relative to infinity ($V_\infty = 0$), so a positive charge gives positive V while an electron gives negative V.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Electric potential can be zero at a point even where the field is non-zero (the equatorial point of a dipole, and the null point of a dipole field). Only the electric field is guaranteed to be non-zero wherever a charge feels a force.  ·  Inside a hollow charged conductor the potential is constant (not zero): V = kQ/R, whereas the electric field there is zero. Zero field does not imply zero potential.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Electron gun in a cathode ray tube: Electrons accelerated through a potential difference V gain kinetic energy eV. For V = 10 kV, each electron gains 10 keV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, which determines the spot size on the fluorescent screen.  ·  Photocell and photoelectric effect: Incoming photons with energies quoted in electron volts (visible light ≈ 1.5–3 eV, UV up to tens of eV) eject photoelectrons only if the photon energy exceeds the work function, the basis of all photoelectric devices.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Believing the electron volt is a unit of charge or potential: The electron volt (eV) is a unit of ENERGY, defined as the energy of a charge of magnitude e accelerated through 1 V. 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.  ·  Computing total potential energy by summing over all ordered pairs (i, j) instead of distinct pairs (i < j): Every interaction must be counted exactly once; summing both $q_i q_j$ and $q_j q_i$ double-counts each pair energy.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive V = kQ/r for an isolated point charge from first principles.  ·  Calculate the potential and potential energy of a two-charge configuration.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Field-to-potential conversion trick: whenever E ∝ 1/r², the corresponding potential is V ∝ 1/r; whenever E ∝ 1/r, the potential is V ∝ ln r.  ·  Sign check: a positive charge always moves toward lower V, while a negative charge moves toward higher V, since force always acts to reduce potential energy.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Define electrostatic potential at a point. State its SI unit and dimensional formula, and explain why electric potential is a scalar while electric field is a vector.  ·  Q2. Derive an expression for the potential at a point due to a point charge Q, and compare its distance dependence with that of the electric field.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Derivation of potential due to a point charge and of potential energy of a charge system, together with the eV-J conversion, forms a frequently asked 5-mark long question in NEB Class 11 Physics.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Definition of electrostatic potential and potential difference with units and dimensions.  ·  Derivation of potential due to a point charge and superposition of potentials.  ·  Field–potential gradient relation E = -∇V.  ·  Potential energy of discrete charge systems and its sign interpretation.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Potential V is work done per unit positive charge; SI unit is volt (1 V = 1 J/C).  ·  Potential is a path-independent scalar; electric field is a vector with direction given by -∇V.  ·  Potential due to a point charge falls as 1/r, while its electric field falls as 1/r².  ·  Like charges give positive U (repulsive, unbound); unlike charges give negative U (attractive, bound).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The electron volt is named after the electron but is a universal energy unit: an alpha particle with charge +2e accelerated through 1 V gains 2 eV, while a proton accelerated through the same 1 V gains 1 eV.  ·  The resting membrane potential of a human nerve axon (about −70 mV measured inside relative to outside) corresponds to a stored energy of roughly 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ J per ion crossing the membrane, which is the physical basis of neural signaling.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. A charge q is brought from infinity to a point in the field of a dipole of moment p placed along the x-axis. Show that the potential energy is $U = -kq p \cos\theta / r^2$.  ·  Q4. An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V. Calculate the energy gained in joules and in electron volts, and the resulting speed. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Nucleosome-free grounding of tall buildings: Lightning-induced potential differences of 10⁸ V are bled harmlessly to earth through lightning rods and thick grounding strips, since $W = qV$ for a large charge at huge potential would otherwise be catastrophic.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: An electron is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. The energy gained in joules is: → B  ·  Two charges +2 μC and -2 μC are separated by 1 m. The potential energy of the system is: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Electrostatic Potential & Potential Difference:** Electric potential at a point P is defined as the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge q₀ from infinity to P against the electrostatic force of the source distribution, without altering the field: $V = \frac{W}{q_0} = -\int_\infty^P \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$.…  ·  **Potential due to an Isolated Point Charge:** For a source charge Q at the origin, the work done in bringing q₀ from infinity to distance r is $W = -\int_\infty^r \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^2} dx = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q q_0}{r}$. Dividing by q₀ gives the potential: $V(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r} = k\frac{Q}{r}$.…  ·  **Relation between Electric Field and Potential Gradient:** The electric field and potential are intrinsically related. Since $V = -\int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}$, we obtain $\vec{E} = -\vec{\nabla}V$. For a uniform field directed along the x-axis: $E = -\frac{dV}{dx}$.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Electron volt as an energy unit and its conversion to joules.  ·  Field–potential link: $\vec{E} = -\vec{\nabla}V$  ·  Potential energy of two charges: $U = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: System potential energy: $U = k\sum_{i<j} \frac{q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}$  ·  Energy–work relation: $\Delta U = -W_{electric}$  ·  Electron volt: $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, an energy unit; 1 MeV = 10⁶ eV is standard in nuclear physics.  ·  Because V depends on position but not on the path taken, a charge can reach a point via any route with identical work done, which is why parallel-plate capacitor calculations ignore the fringing geometry at the edges.  ·  The SI unit of potential is the volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J/C, and its dimensional formula is [M L² T⁻³ I⁻¹], identical to that of energy per unit charge.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 1: Electric potential at a point is defined as the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point.  ·  Statement 2: The potential due to a point charge varies inversely with distance (V ∝ 1/r), whereas the electric field varies inversely with distance squared (E ∝ 1/r²).  ·  Statement 3: The electric field at any point is the negative gradient of the potential at that point (E = -∇V).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 4: The potential energy of two like charges is positive, indicating a repulsive, unbound configuration, whereas for two unlike charges it is negative, indicating an attractive, bound configuration.  ·  Statement 5: One electron volt is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of one volt, equal to 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.  ·  eV conversion: multiply eV by 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ to get joules, or divide joules by 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ to get eV.
